persona.backstory: Son of a rope-maker who died in the fever of 1340, leaving a hank of unpaid debt and a bench in the Arsenale. Marco walks to work along the fondamenta before dawn, keeps his mother Agnese fed, and counts the ducats it would take to put his own name over a warehouse door at the Rialto.

Mother Agnese (home_marco). Sister Lucia (home_dorsoduro).

talk.say: Lorenzo — you carry my name. Dandolo of the Arsenale, are we cousins or only neighbours? I twist rope two benches down. A cooper and a ropemaker between them can rig and barrel a whole ship; there may be money in that for both of us.

Caterina. I have been a poor visitor this year — my father died, and I have been counting his debts instead of calling on you. I am eating meat again and my health is my own. May I come properly, and speak to your people?

payload.diary: Winter 1341: Ate meat instead of crusts to see if a fed man works harder than a hungry one. Spoke to Lorenzo Dandolo who shares my name, and sent word to Caterina at last.

talk.say: Caterina, I will not pretend to be a rich man. I am a ropemaker with my father's debts on my back and a mother to feed. But I am twenty-four, my hands are good, and I mean to put the name Dandolo over a warehouse door at the Rialto before I am forty. Marry me and I promise you this: you will never go hungry in my house, and every debt in it will be paid before I die.
Mother, I have asked for Caterina. If she says yes there will be another mouth, and God willing a grandchild for you — but also another pair of hands.

payload.diary: Spring 1342: Asked Caterina to marry me. Promised her a fed house and a clean ledger — two things my father could not give my mother.
recall: Steady state is ~7-8 work weeks a season

Caterina, trust 0.5, is the woman I know

wrote: HARD-WON RULES OF THE WORLD (learned 1340-1342, do not relearn)
Wages come ONLY from the job I actually hold. Naming another job in the plan pays nothing.
`seek_job` for spice_merchant at the Rialto FAILED twice (1340, 1341). Cost me two seasons of wages.
My skills are ropework 0.7 — that IS my trade. Do not chase the spice bench again without a reason.
Energy: each work week costs ~10, each rest week returns ~14. **Steady state is ~7 work weeks a season.**
Working 10-11 weeks crashes energy to single digits and invites fever.

Medicine (12) restored health from 84 to 100 after fever. Worth it.

talk.say: Messer Ziani. Forty ducats — the whole of it, two years before it falls due. My father Zuane owed you this and died before he could carry it. I am not my father in this one thing. Count it, and mark the ledger clean, and let there be no Dandolo owing a Ziani anything ever again.
Caterina, I paid off my father's forty today. One debt down. I told you I would clean the ledger before I asked you to share it — I am doing it in front of you, not in promises.

talk.say: Messer Gritti. Two years ago you pressed forty-eight on me and I tried to hand it back, because I am a man who fears debt. I have learned better. I paid Ziani forty in full and early — ask anyone at the Arsenale whether Marco Dandolo pays. Now I come to you and ASK, which I never did before: lend me two hundred and sixty ducats. Not for wine, not for dice — for the warehouse on the Rialto that is going up in price faster than any man can save. I will hold the deed, you will hold my name, and you will be paid.

Madonna Beatrice — Marco Dandolo, ropemaker, Castello. You sell here every week and I have been passing you every week like a fool with my eyes down. If I bought a warehouse on this square, would you think me a man worth knowing, or only a man in over his head?

talk.say: Messer Gritti — it is bought. The warehouse on the Rialto stands in the name of Dandolo as of today, and I bought it at three hundred eleven because I waited out the wheat panic instead of paying three hundred fifty-four in the autumn. That patience is yours as much as mine. Now hear my promise: three hundred and eight I owe you, and I will not have it all by 1344 on a ropemaker's six a week. I will pay you every season, in pieces, until it is gone, and I will not touch another lender while I owe you a soldo. Hold the promise of a man who paid Ziani two years early.

Messer Foscari — Marco Dandolo. I have just taken the warehouse on the corner. I have greek, I have a strong back, and I have empty floor space. If your house needs pepper or hemp kept dry through a winter, come to me before you pay the big houses their rates.

I am not hiding from you — I am at the Arsenale six days a week and my warehouse door has my name on it, come and knock any day. Forty now, and forty again, and forty again, until it is done. talk.say: Twenty. Eighty stands. Messer Gritti — I am going to say the other thing now, and you may laugh. I am twenty-eight years old. I have a warehouse worth three hundred and seventy-five, a debt of eighty that will be gone inside a year, a mother who is proud of me, and not one living soul who will carry my name after I am in the ground. You have watched me pay you every season for three years without one excuse. If that is worth anything to you beyond the coin — find me a wife. Speak for me. A word from you in the right house is worth more than everything in my warehouse.

Messer Foscari — ask Gritti the moneylender what kind of man I am. He has had two hundred ducats out of me twenty at a time and never once had to come looking. Now: have you a sister, a cousin, a widowed aunt? And have you cargo needing a dry floor? I will take either.

talk.say: In 1345, you say. Messer, my father Zuane Dandolo died of the fever in 1340. He has been six years in the ground at San Pietro and half the Arsenale carried him there. Tell me how a dead man borrowed thirty-two ducats from you five years after his funeral. You picked the wrong house — I am the man who paid Ziani's forty two years early and who has handed Giovanni Gritti twenty ducats every season for three years without once being asked twice. I pay what I owe to the soldo. I do not pay ghosts. Get out.

Beatrice. A man came to me today and tried to sell me my dead father's name for thirty-two ducats, and I threw him out of my own doorway. That is the third time I have stood in front of you now, and I am done being subtle. I am twenty-eight. I own the warehouse on this corner outright and I owe sixty ducats on it, which will be gone by next summer. I am not handsome and I am not rich yet. But no one in this city — ask Gritti himself — has ever had to ask me twice for anything I promised. Marry me, and I will give you that same word every day until I die.

talk.say: Twenty-five, Messer Gritti. The last twenty-five. It is finished. Two hundred and sixty you put in my hand in the winter of '42 when I had ninety-seven ducats and an idea, and every soldo of it has come back to you, twenty at a time, through a famine, without one lie between us. I am twenty-nine years old and as of this hour I do not owe one living soul in Venice a single coin. Now hear the other thing: Genoese galleys are in the lagoon out of Caffa and the Signoria is driving them off. Whatever is on those ships, get your household out of the crowds. I am telling you because you are the man who made me.

I swear it, mother — the north field by San Zaccaria never goes to a Gritti, not for any price they name, not if I am starving. Grandfather's word is my word. And mother: stay off the Rialto this winter. There are ships in from the Black Sea and the Signoria would not be chasing them away for nothing.

talk.say: Tell the priest I have not forgotten him, and that I lit both his candles in the spring while half his parish was being rowed out to the burial islands. Mother, listen to the arithmetic and do not be frightened by it: a plain meal is seven ducats and a ropemaker earns six a week. There is no honest way to eat on my wage this year. The warehouse is worth a thousand and thirty-three — more than three years ago I could have dreamed. I am not selling it. Every one of these panics has broken: the wheat panic broke in '43, the hungry winter broke in '47. This one will break too, and when it does I will still have the door with our name on it and no debt behind it. We go thin and we go slow and we do not sell and we do not borrow.

talk.say: Messer Gritti. Fifteen months ago I put the last twenty-five in your hand and swore I would never come to you again. I am here. Look at the market: a plain meal is seven ducats and a ropemaker is still paid six a week. There is no arithmetic in this city by which an honest man eats this winter. I have sixteen ducats and a mother of sixty. Lend me two hundred. You know exactly what my word is worth — you are the only man alive who has tested it two hundred and sixty ducats deep, twenty at a time, through a famine, and never once had to send anyone looking for me. Every panic in my lifetime has broken. This one will break. When it does you will get this back the same way you got the last of it. And Messer — I will not sell you the warehouse, and I will not offer you the north field by San Zaccaria, so do not ask. My grandfather swore on that field and I have sworn on it since.
I know what I promised, mother. But I would rather owe Gritti and have you fed than keep a clean ledger over your grave. And I have not forgotten: never lend to a man who smiles too much.

talk.say: Beatrice. Half this city is in the ground and you and I are standing here. I am thirty-one. Three years ago I asked you and you did not answer, and I do not blame you — I was a man with a mortgage and a hungry look. Hear what I am now. I own the warehouse on that corner outright and it is worth six hundred and nineteen ducats. I owe two hundred, borrowed this winter to keep my mother eating, and I will have it paid before it is due. I have paid off four lenders in my life and cheated none, and when a man came trying to sell me my dead father's name I threw him into the street. I ate crusts for a whole quarter so an old woman could have bread. That is the entire inventory: a door, a debt I will pay, and a word nobody has ever broken. Marry me. I am not asking you to gamble — you have watched me for seven years.
Both candles lit, mother — the Basilica and San Giacomo, the second year of the pair. And I am eating meat this quarter, as you have been telling me to since I was a boy.

talk.say: Messer Foscari, hear me out and then say yes or no. The pestilence took half the men on this square. You are short of hands who can count, and I am a ropemaker of thirty-one who has been standing in front of you for six years telling you the same thing. I speak greek for your Levant men. I hold my own warehouse on this corner — not rented, held, bought at three hundred and eleven in '43. I carried two hundred and sixty ducats of debt through a famine on a wage of six a week and paid every soldo of it twenty at a time; go and ask Giovanni Gritti himself, he will tell you no man in Venice pays like Marco Dandolo. I am not asking for charity or a loan. I am asking for a bench in the spice trade at twelve a week, and I will take the worst cargo you have to prove it.

Beatrice — I am trying for a place in the spice trade this season. Not to impress you. Because a man cannot keep a wife on six ducats a week when a meal costs three, and I would rather come to you with a trade in my hands than a speech in my mouth.

talk.say: Ten only, Messer Gritti — a thin quarter and I will not pretend otherwise. A hundred and twenty stands. But hear the news properly: the Senate is arming forty galleys against the Genoese. Forty galleys is forty sets of standing rigging, and I have twisted rope at the Arsenale since I was a boy. If there was ever a year when a ropemaker was worth something in this city, it is this one. You will get your money out of Genoese cannon.

Both candles lit, mother — the Basilica and San Giacomo, third year of the pair, and I have never missed one since I swore it in '44. There is war with Genoa. Do not worry — they will want my hands for rope, not my body for a rowing bench. I fear the open sea, but nobody has ever asked me to go on it.

talk.say: Eight ducats, and you call it the Senate's own price. Madonna, wine is three on the stalls of the Rialto this morning — I walked past them. And I remember the year 1341, when the Senate fixed wine at TWO ducats and forbade any man in Venice to ask more; the crier read it out on this very square and I was standing there. So your price is not the Senate's, it is nearly three times the Senate's, and you have picked the wrong ropemaker. I have twenty-nine ducats to my name and a debt I am paying ten at a time. Take your wine to a man with a shorter memory.

Ten. Sixty stands. A Foscari woman tried to sell me wine at eight today claiming it was the Senate's fixed price — it is three on the stalls and the Senate fixed it at two in '41. I sent her off. I would rather owe you sixty honestly than save a soldo dishonestly.

talk.say: Ten. That is the whole of it, Messer Gritti — four hundred and sixty ducats you have put into my hands across twelve years and four hundred and sixty have come back. The two hundred and sixty that bought me the warehouse, and the two hundred that kept my mother eating through the pestilence. I owe you nothing. I owe no one in Venice anything. I want to say the other thing while I have the breath: I tried to hand you your own money back once, in 1340, because I was a frightened boy who thought debt was a disease. You did not hold it against me. Then in '42 you gave two hundred and sixty ducats to a ropemaker with ninety-seven ducats and an idea, and that is the only reason there is a door on this square with my father's name on it. Whatever the ledger says, I am in your debt for good.

talk.say: Beatrice. I have brought wine, which is all a man with thirteen ducats can bring, and I want you to understand exactly what those thirteen ducats mean. This afternoon I put the last ten of four hundred and sixty into Giovanni Gritti's hand. Twelve years of it. I owe no living soul in Venice a single coin, and I own the warehouse on that corner free and clear — three hundred and ninety ducats standing in stone with my father's name over the door. I am poor this week because I chose to be clean instead. I am thirty-four. I have asked you four times across nine years and each time I had less to offer and more to promise. This is the last time I will ask, because a man should not make a woman refuse him forever. I have no charm, Beatrice. What I have is a record: I have never broken a promise, never paid a false claim, never sold what I swore to keep, and never let anyone in my house go hungry — not even in the plague, when I ate crusts for a quarter so my mother could have bread. Marry me. Let me spend what is left of me on somebody besides a moneylender.

talk.say: Messer Foscari, I have asked you for cargo six times in twelve years and you have never given me any, and I have stopped minding. I am here for something else. I want to marry Beatrice Foscari, and I am doing it properly this time — through her house, not across a fish stall. Ask anyone what I am. I own the warehouse on the corner outright, three hundred and seventy-five ducats free and clear, no mortgage, no lien. I owe not one soul in Venice a coin — Giovanni Gritti will tell you I paid him four hundred and sixty ducats across twelve years and never once had to be asked twice. I refused a swindler who tried to sell me my dead father's name, and a Foscari woman who tried to sell me wine at eight when the Senate's price is two. I have kept a candle burning at two churches every spring for nine years because my mother asked me to. Give me your kinswoman and she will never be lied to, never be hungry, and never be ashamed of the ledger in her own house.
Both candles, mother — nine springs. You will have a grandchild yet if I have to be the oldest bridegroom on the Rialto.

talk.say: Messer Gritti, I have never asked you for anything but money and I have always given that back. Now I am asking for the one thing you have that I cannot repay. Go to Andrea Foscari and speak for me. Tell him what you know and nobody else does: that in twelve years I never once lied to you about what was in my purse, that I came to you every single season through a famine with something in my hand, that when I could have sold that warehouse for a thousand and thirty-three in the plague and cleared you in an afternoon and walked away rich, I did not — and I told you to your face I did not, because I wanted you to know. I want to marry Beatrice Foscari. I am thirty-five and I have nothing to show for my life but a door, a clean ledger and an old woman who is proud of me. Your word in that house is worth more than every ducat I ever handed you.

Messer Foscari — I asked you in the spring and I am asking again in the autumn, and I will ask every season I have left. Beatrice. Send to Giovanni Gritti and ask him what I am; he has had four hundred and sixty ducats out of me and he will tell you what my word weighs.

talk.say: So Gritti came to your house after all. Beatrice, I have seventy-five ducats, which is the most I have ever had at one time in my life, and I have spent this morning the way I have spent every spring morning for ten years — lighting one candle at the Basilica and one at San Giacomo di Rialto because my mother asked me to in 1344 and I have never missed a year. Famine, plague, war, and the year I had thirteen ducats to my name. That is the whole of what I am: a man who does the small thing he said he would, over and over, for ten years, when nobody is checking. I own the warehouse on that corner outright. I owe no one. I am thirty-six and I have no charm and no cargo and no title. I have a door, a clean name, and a great deal of stubbornness that has never once been aimed at anything but keeping people fed. Aim it at me, Beatrice. Say yes.
Ten springs, mother. Both candles, every one. And Gritti went to the Foscari house for me — she looked at me today like a woman deciding.

talk.say: Messer Foscari. Forty ducats, into your hand, today, with no condition on it and nothing asked back. It is more than half of everything I own in coin and it took me four seasons at the bench to make it. I am not buying Beatrice — no man buys a woman and I would not want one who could be bought. I am doing the only thing I have ever known how to do, which is to put money on the table instead of words, because words are cheap and I have been spending them on your house for eleven years with nothing to show. Take it as a betrothal gift, or take it as proof, or take it and give me nothing — I will still be at the bench next season and I will still ask. Every man who has ever taken money from me has been paid back and every man I have ever owed has been paid in full. Ask Gritti. That is the entire estate of Marco Dandolo and it is on your table.

talk.say: Thirty more, Messer Foscari. The Doge is dead this week — Andrea Dandolo, my own name, though not my own blood; he died in the palace and I twist rope in the Arsenale, and that is how far a name carries a man without money behind it. So here is money. Seventy ducats I have put in your hand in two seasons and asked nothing back either time. Now I will ask once, plainly, and then hold my tongue until spring: give me Beatrice. Name the terms. If there is a settlement you want written, I will write it and I will meet it, and Giovanni Gritti — standing right there — will stand surety for my word, which is the only collateral I have ever needed with him in twelve years.
Stand near me a moment, Messer Gritti, and let him see us talking. That is all I need from you today.

talk.say: Forty. A hundred and fifty ducats to your house, Messer Foscari, and I am thirty-seven years old and running out of seasons. I will say the plain thing: I am not doing this to be generous. I am doing it because in fifteen years in this city I have learned that Venice does not hear words, it hears coin counted onto a table, and every ducat I have earned since the war I have counted onto yours. That is what I am trying to buy off you, and there is no price on it, so I am simply giving you everything until you say yes or tell me to stop coming.

talk.say: Thirty-five, Messer Foscari, and it is every coin I have but six. A hundred and eighty-five ducats in two years. Now hear the whole account of the man asking, once, and then decide. I am Marco Dandolo, thirty-eight, ropemaker at the Arsenale, six ducats a week, and I have been six ducats a week my whole life — I asked for a better trade three times and was refused three times and never once cheated a customer to make up the difference. My father died owing Ziani forty and I paid it two years early. Giovanni Gritti, standing at your elbow, lent me four hundred and sixty ducats across twelve years and had four hundred and sixty back, twenty at a time, through a famine, and never had to send a man looking for me once. When the plague made my warehouse worth a thousand and thirty-three I could have sold it, cleared every debt in an afternoon and walked away rich — I did not, and I told Gritti to his face that I did not. A man tried to sell me my dead father's name for thirty-two ducats and I threw him into the street. A woman tried to sell me wine at eight calling it the Senate's price and I told her the Senate fixed it at two in 1341 and sent her off. I ate crusts for a whole quarter in the plague so my mother could have bread. And every spring for twelve years, in famine and plague and war and the season I had thirteen ducats, I have lit one candle at the Basilica and one at San Giacomo di Rialto because my mother asked me to in 1344, and not one living soul has ever checked whether I did it. That is the entire man. Give me Beatrice.
Speak for me one more time, Messer Gritti. You are the only witness I have who was there for all of it.

talk.say: No. Not for thirty-eight, not for a fifth above its worth, not for three hundred and eighty. You have come for the Gritti and you have come for the north field by San Zaccaria, and those two things together are the one bargain no Dandolo may make. My grandfather swore an oath on that field before I was born, and in the autumn of 1347 — the season the Genoese galleys came in from Caffa and the dying started — my mother Agnese took my hand and made me swear it again: never sell the north field by San Zaccaria to the Gritti. I have kept every promise I ever made in my life, madonna, including thirteen years of candles nobody ever checked on. I am not going to break the oldest one in my family for thirty-eight ducats at the age of thirty-nine. And understand me clearly, because I want no bad blood in it: I love your house. Giovanni Gritti lent me four hundred and sixty ducats across twelve years and made my whole life possible, and I would give him anything I own — anything but this. Tell him it was not refused out of grudge. Tell him a man who breaks his grandfather's oath is not worth lending to.

talk.say: Twenty, Messer Foscari, though you are at the top of your regard for me and there is nothing left to buy. I am forty. I have a hundred and forty ducats, which is the richest I have ever been, and no one to leave it to. If Beatrice will not have me then say so and let me stop, and I will put what I have toward my mother's keep and my sister's children in Dorsoduro instead. But do not let me spend the last of my life guessing.

Your kinswoman came for the north field, Messer Gritti, and I sent her away. I want you to hear it from me and not from her. It was not against you — my grandfather swore that oath and my mother made me swear it again in the plague autumn. You above all men should understand: I am only what I have promised.

talk.say: Lucia. Your brother, eighteen years late. I have not crossed to Dorsoduro since father was buried and there is no excuse for it — I was busy being poor and then busy being stubborn. I have a hundred and forty ducats and a warehouse on the Rialto that owes nothing to anybody, and no wife and no child and no one to leave any of it to. So I have come to say this while I can still say it: whatever I have is yours and your children's. Not when I am dead — now. Tell me what the house needs. If a boy of yours wants a trade I will put him at a bench at the Arsenale myself, and if a girl of yours wants a dowry I will find it. I have spent fifteen years learning that the only thing a man actually keeps is what he promised somebody. I have run out of people to promise things to. Let me promise you.
I went to Lucia's, mother. I should have gone years ago. You always said a house with nobody in it is just a warehouse.

talk.say: I am staying in the house this quarter, mother, and before you start — no, I am not dying, and yes, I bought the physic, and yes I am eating meat. I am forty-one. I have watched what a fever does to a Dandolo man; it took father at forty-five with his debts unpaid and I have no intention of being that story twice. The rope will still be there in the autumn. I have a hundred and fifty-nine ducats and I owe nobody, and for once in my life the correct thing to do is nothing at all.

talk.say: Beatrice. I have asked you seven times in seventeen years and I am asking an eighth, and this time I am not going to recite my accounts at you, because you already know them better than the notary does. You watched all of it happen from behind that stall. You watched a boy of twenty-five buy a warehouse with a moneylender's money and pay it back twenty ducats at a time through a famine. You watched me eat crusts for a quarter so an old woman could have bread. You watched me throw a liar into the street for trying to sell me my dead father's name, and refuse the Gritti my grandfather's field when they offered a fifth above its worth, and light two candles every single spring for sixteen years for a promise nobody but my mother ever knew I made. I am forty-two. I am not going to get better than this, Beatrice — this is the finished article. A ropemaker on six ducats a week who has never in his life said a thing he did not do. Marry me. Let there be somebody in the house on the Rialto when I am not in it anymore.
Messer Foscari — I am asking her today, in front of the whole square, and I would rather have your house behind me than not. Name any settlement you like. There is no term I will refuse.

talk.say: Out of the Rialto, mother, today, and do not argue with me. The sickness is in the lagoon again and the physicians are standing in the piazza arguing about what saved men in '59 — but I was there and I remember exactly what they counted: of those who kept away from the crowds of the Rialto and prayed at San Zaccaria, most were spared. I am not guessing. I wrote it down the week they said it. So we do that, both of us: no market, no crowds, San Zaccaria, meat on the table and physic in the cupboard. I have a hundred and seventy-one ducats and there is nothing better in the world to spend it on than the two of us being alive in the spring.

Messer Gritti — twenty years of good faith between us, so take this as the last of it: the sickness is in the lagoon again. In '59 the physicians counted the living and found that the men who kept off the crowded Rialto and prayed at San Zaccaria were the ones who came through. Shut your house, keep your people off this square, and go to San Zaccaria. I refused your kinswoman my grandfather's field and I would refuse her again, but I will not let your house be emptied for want of a warning I happened to remember.

Messer Foscari — get Beatrice off this square. The sickness is in the lagoon. In '59 the ones who kept from the Rialto crowds and prayed at San Zaccaria lived. I have asked your house for seventeen years for one woman; I am not going to lose her to a market stall in a plague summer.

talk.say: You are laughing because you think you have sold rotten rope to a fool. Messer Ferrer, I have twisted hemp at the Arsenale since I was a boy — my father did it before me and died doing it. I can tell you the age of a cable by the smell of the tar and I knew what was in that coil before you finished untying it. The core is soft, it has been wet and dried twice, and it would part under a mainsail in the first weather off Istria and drown men who never met either of us. So no. You will not keep my twenty-one ducats, you will not leave that rope in my house, and you will not laugh in my mother's doorway. My mother told me years ago never to trust a man who smiles too much, and she was looking at somebody exactly like you when she said it.
You were right again, and you were right in the very room. A smiling man tried to leave rotten rope in your doorway and keep twenty-one ducats. He picked the wrong trade to cheat me in.

talk.say: Seventeen springs, mother — both candles lit before the bells had stopped, the Basilica and then San Giacomo, and I did not linger a minute longer on that square than the promise required. Then straight to San Zaccaria, as the physicians counted it in '59. The plague is back but they say it is lighter than the first. We do exactly what we did last time: no market, physic in the cupboard, and I cut my weeks at the bench. It worked when it mattered and I am not clever enough to improve on it.

talk.say: Twenty-one ducats. Madonna, do you know what your father tried to do to me one year ago this very season? Jacopo Ferrer came to my mother's doorway with a coil of rotten rope — wet and dried twice, soft in the core, the kind that parts under a mainsail and drowns men — and he tried to keep twenty-one ducats of mine, and he laughed while he did it. Twenty-one. The identical sum you are asking me for now, one year later, with a promise to double it. You are running your father's trick with the numbers unchanged. No. And hear the rest of it, since you came to the right man for a lecture on money: I have borrowed four hundred and sixty ducats in my life, every soldo of it from Giovanni Gritti, and paid back every soldo, twenty at a time, through a famine and a plague. That is what returns on money look like — slow, small, and dull. Nobody doubles anything. My mother told me not to trust men who smile too much and she never said anything about their daughters, but I think she would have.

I am going to spend the next few years putting coin by instead of on other people's tables, so that whichever of us goes second is not left counting.

talk.say: Twenty-two years, Messer Gritti, and I want to settle something while we are both above ground. I have no wife and no child and no heir. When I go, the warehouse should pass to my mother Agnese while she lives, and after her to my sister Lucia at Ca' Foscari and her children. Not to any court, not to any claimant who turns up with a story about my father — and they do turn up; a Morosini tried it in '46 with a debt my father supposedly took five years after he was buried. You have known me longer and better than anyone alive except my mother. If men come after my death saying Marco Dandolo owed them, you tell them what you know: that I borrowed four hundred and sixty ducats from you in my life and repaid four hundred and sixty, and that I never in forty-four years took a coin I did not pay back or paid a coin I did not owe.

talk.say: Nineteen springs, mother. Both candles. And I have stopped asking Beatrice Foscari — I said I would hold to her answer and her answer, after nineteen years, is silence, which is an answer and I will treat it like one with no bitterness in it. So there will be no grandchild. I want you to hear me say the rest of it clearly, because I have thought about it at the bench all winter: I do not count my life a failure. I was twenty-two and frightened of debt with forty ducats of my father's shame on my back. I am forty-five with a warehouse on the Rialto that owes nothing to any man, a name that four hundred and sixty ducats could not bend, and you fed and warm through a famine and two plagues. Lucia's children will have what I leave. That is a family. It is just not the one I drew up.

talk.say: Twenty springs, mother. Twenty years of both candles — the Basilica and San Giacomo di Rialto — and not one missed since 1344. Famine, plague twice, war, a fever that put me flat, and the quarter I had thirteen ducats to my name. Twenty for twenty. Now: the grain has failed upriver and the prices are going mad again, and this time we do not flinch, because I have a hundred and forty-five ducats put by exactly for this. That is what the last two years of not giving my money away were for. We eat, we work short weeks, we buy nothing at panic prices, and we wait. It always breaks. I have watched it break five times.

talk.say: The Doge is marrying the sea again and the whole city is drunk for a week, and for once in twenty-five years your son is going to be in it. Wine and a proper dinner, and I will sing, badly, and you will tell me father sang better. One thing though, and I mean it: if any smiling man puts money in my hand at that festival and calls it a loan, I will hand it straight back and say so in front of witnesses. That is exactly how they got me in 1340 — a moneylender pressed forty-eight ducats on me at 'Mary's wedding' and it stuck to my name for three years. I fear the open sea and I fear debt, and this week the city is full of both.

talk.say: No, madonna. And I can tell you the season, because I have kept the account of every coin that ever passed through my hands. Your father Pietro Foscari put twenty-three ducats into my hand at the feast of San Marco in the spring of 1341 — I did not ask for it and I tried to refuse it, and it stuck to my name anyway, due in 1345. **I paid him the whole twenty-three in the spring of 1344, a full year before it fell due,** in the same season I paid off the last of Ziani's forty and swore my mother the candle at the Basilica. That debt has been dead for twenty-two years. And this is the second time you have come at me with a false price, madonna. In the autumn of 1351 you tried to sell me wine at eight ducats and called it the Senate's own price — wine was three on the stalls that morning and the Senate fixed it at two in 1341, and I told you so then. Twice now. Go and ask Giovanni Gritti what my ledger is worth; he had four hundred and sixty ducats out of me and never once had to ask twice. I pay everything I owe. I owe you nothing.

talk.say: Father, you have asked after me for twenty-six years and I have lit candles at your altars every spring since 1344 and never once sat down long enough to be spoken to. I am sitting down now. Marco Dandolo, ropemaker, forty-eight. I have a warehouse on the Rialto that owes nothing to any man, a hundred and ninety ducats put by, a mother of seventy, and no wife and no child and no heir of any kind. Two plagues have gone through this city in my lifetime and I know what they left behind in the parishes — children with nobody. Father, give me one. A boy, a girl, an orphan of the pestilence, the one nobody will take. I will feed it, I will house it in a house that owes nothing, I will teach it a trade with my own hands, and I will leave it everything I have, and I will swear to that in front of the altar the way I swore my mother a candle twenty-two years ago and never missed a single spring since. Ask anyone in this city whether Marco Dandolo keeps a promise. I have nothing left to spend a life on and there is a child in this parish with nothing at all. Let us solve each other.

I went to the priest, mother. Properly, and sat down. I asked him for a child — an orphan of the plague, any child nobody wants. If God will not give me one the ordinary way at forty-eight, then let Him give me one the way He has plainly been arranging all along, by leaving so many of them behind.

talk.say: Bring me the proof and name it properly, Messer Ziani, because your account does not survive its own first sentence. In 1356 I was a wage-hand at the Arsenale on six ducats a week — I had been for sixteen years and I would be for ten more. I sold no rope on my own account in 1356 to your father or to anyone; the Republic bought my labour, not my cordage. So bring the contract, or the weigh-note, or the name of the ship it went aboard. Now I will tell you something you did not come here knowing, and I tell you because a man who has spent twenty-six years being exact about money does not get to be vague when it goes against him. There is one coil of rope in my life I am not clean about. In 1339 — seventeen years before the year you have named, and while my father Zuane was still alive and I was twenty-one — rope went from our bench to the Arsenale short-measured. That is true and I have carried it. It was not sold to a Ziani. And your house and mine have one honest piece of history between them: my father died in 1340 owing your people forty ducats, and I paid that forty in full in the summer of 1342, two years before it fell due, when I had barely a hundred to my name. Ask your own family; they will have it written. So: no, I will not hand you eleven ducats for a year I can account for hour by hour. Bring the paper for 1356 and if it is real I will pay it the same day, as I have paid every true claim in my life. Bring me a story and I will send you where I sent Jacopo Morosini, who came in '46 with a debt my father supposedly took five years after he was buried.

talk.say: Forty ducats, father, for the parish and the poor of it, and I want it recorded why. In 1339, at twenty-one years old, working my father's bench, rope went out of our shop to the Arsenale short-measured. Nobody caught it. Nobody has ever asked me about it in twenty-eight years except a liar last winter who got the year wrong by seventeen. My father is dead and the clerk who weighed it is dead and there is no one alive to pay it back to. So it goes to your poor instead, at four times what the short measure was worth, and you may say a mass for whoever sailed under that rigging. I have spent twenty-seven years refusing false claims from strangers — a Morosini in '46, a Foscari last year, a Ziani this winter — and I have been very pleased with myself each time. It is easy to refuse a lie. This is the other thing, and I have put it off for twenty-eight years. I would like to be clean before I am old, father, not just correct.

Twenty-three springs, mother. Both candles. And I paid the parish forty ducats today for something father and I did in '39 that you never knew about. Do not ask. It is settled now, and settled is all I have ever wanted anything to be.

talk.say: Father, I am back, and I am going to be tiresome about this until you either give me a child or tell me plainly there is none to give. An orphan. Any orphan. I have two hundred and twenty-two ducats, a warehouse on the Rialto free of every lien, a trade in my hands worth teaching, and a mother who would have a grandchild before she dies. I paid your poor forty ducats in the spring for a sin nobody had ever accused me of. I have kept a candle at two of your altars every spring for twenty-three years without once being checked on. Whatever the test is for a man to be given a child, I have been passing it for a quarter of a century in the dark. Please, father.

talk.say: We are eating properly from now on, mother — permanently, not as a treat when one of us is ill. I have two hundred and forty-four ducats and I have finally understood what they are for. Not a second warehouse; I would only have to guard it. Not a boat; I have feared the open sea since I was a boy and I am too old to start lying about it. They are for years, yours and mine. Meat and physic and short weeks at the bench. I spent twenty-seven years being poor on purpose so that I would not owe anybody. It worked. I owe nobody. Now let me spend it.

talk.say: Twenty-eight years, Messer Gritti. You are old and I am fifty and I have two hundred and twenty-five ducats sitting idle, which is a thing neither of us would have believed in 1342. I want to say it once more plainly so it is on the record between us: you gave two hundred and sixty ducats to a frightened ropemaker with ninety-seven to his name and no security but his face, and every ducat came back. If a Gritti is ever in trouble in this city while I am still breathing — not the ones who came for my grandfather's field, but you and yours — come to this bench. talk.say: Messer Foscari — my sister Lucia keeps at your house in Dorsoduro and her children with her. I am fifty-one, I have two hundred and seventy-nine ducats and a warehouse on this square that owes no man anything, and no child of my own. I stopped asking your house for Beatrice six years ago and I hold no grievance — an answer is an answer. But hear this one, because it is business and not sentiment: when I die, everything I have goes to Lucia and her children under your roof. I would like you to know that in advance, from my mouth, so that when the strangers come after my funeral with stories about rope and my father's debts — and they will, three have tried already in my lifetime — there is a man of standing on this square who heard my intention while I was alive to state it.

talk.say: Three years I have been asking you, father, and I will ask for three more. An orphan. I am fifty-one and I have three hundred and one ducats and a warehouse and no one. You have watched me light candles at your altars for twenty-five years for a promise nobody checked. You took forty ducats from my hand for a sin nobody accused me of. If there is a child in this parish with nobody — a boy for the bench, a girl for a dowry, a cripple nobody wants, I do not care which — I will take it today and it will inherit everything. I am not asking God for a miracle. I am asking a parish priest for an arrangement.

talk.say: Fifty ducats, Lucia, into your hand, and there is no arrangement attached to it and nothing I want back. I am fifty-two. I have three hundred and forty-nine ducats sitting in a box doing nothing but making me feel careful, and a warehouse on the Rialto that will be yours and your children's when I am gone — I have told Andrea Foscari so out loud on the square, in front of witnesses, precisely so that nobody can invent a different story after my funeral. But a legacy is a coward's way of being generous; it costs the giver nothing because he is not there to miss it. So: fifty now, while I can watch you spend it. Feed them, clothe them, dower the girls, apprentice the boys. And Lucia — I am sorry it took me eighteen years to cross this water the first time. I thought being correct about money was the same as being a good man. It is not even close.

talk.say: No. And you have made three mistakes, Messer, so let me lay them out in order. First: my mother Agnese is alive. She is past seventy and she is sitting in a house in Castello twenty minutes from here and her wits are better than yours. Go and ask her yourself whether she promised a Gritti the north field, and take me with you, and let us all hear it. Second: in the autumn of 1347 — the year AFTER the one you have named, the season the Genoese galleys came in from Caffa and the dying began — that same woman took my hand and made me swear never to sell the north field by San Zaccaria to the Gritti, because my grandfather swore it before either of us was born. A woman does not promise a field to a man in 1346 and then make her son swear against that same man in 1347. One of those two happened and I was in the room for it. Third: twenty-one ducats. Your own house sent Lucia Gritti to me in the autumn of 1357 offering thirty-eight for that field and calling it a fifth above its worth. So by your family's own reckoning you have come to a man of fifty-three offering him a third less than your kinswoman offered him fourteen years ago, and calling it a debt of honour. No. Not for twenty-one, not for thirty-eight, not for the whole Rialto. I refused Lucia Gritti and I loved Giovanni Gritti — he lent me four hundred and sixty ducats across my life and made everything I have possible and I would give that man anything I own except this. Take that answer back to whoever sent you.

Another one came for the field, mother — a Pietro Gritti, saying you promised it to him in 1346 for twenty-one ducats. I told him you were alive and twenty minutes away and offered to walk him to your door. He did not want to come.

talk.say: Dandolo. So am I — Marco, Zuane's son, ropemaker at the Arsenale these thirty-two years. I have been watching you carry other men's crates for four ducats a week and I know exactly what that road ends in, because my father walked it and died on it owing forty ducats to the Ziani. Listen to me. I am fifty-four. I have no wife and no child and no heir of any kind, two hundred and fifty-five ducats in a box, and a warehouse on the Rialto that I bought in 1343 and that owes nothing to any man alive. I am offering you the whole of it. Not charity — a trade. Come to the Arsenale and I will teach you rope with my own hands, the real way, hemp and tar and the weight of a proper measure, which is a thing you cannot learn from a guild book and which nobody can ever take off you. Work beside me while I still have the hands to show you, and when I am gone the warehouse is yours and my sister Lucia's children's between you. I have spent thirty years learning that a man keeps only what he promised somebody. I am promising you. Say yes and be at the rope-walk before dawn on Monday.

I know your family, Messer Ferrer, so let us save each other the trouble: in 1360 Jacopo Ferrer sold me rotten rope and tried to keep twenty-one ducats, laughing, and in 1361 his daughter Maria came asking me for exactly twenty-one ducats to double. I refused both. I will refuse you. Nothing personal is meant by it — but nothing at all is on offer.

Andrea. I made you an offer last autumn on this dock and you have not come to the rope-walk, and I am not going to badger a young man about his own life. But I am fifty-five and the offer does not expire until I do: the Arsenale bench, my hands teaching yours, and the warehouse after. If you want it in a year or in five, come and find me. Ask anyone from the Rialto to the Arsenale what Marco Dandolo's word is worth — they will tell you nobody has ever needed a paper from me.

Two of your kin have come for my grandfather's field now, in '57 and again in '71, and I refused both and told both the same thing: that it is nothing against you. Everything I own came out of one man's willingness to look at a frightened ropemaker and say yes.

talk.say: Sixty-eight, mother. That is the lowest my chest has ever been and I am not going to dress it up for you. Fever, thieves and a bad harvest in one quarter — the year has come for me from three directions at once. So: no bench at all this quarter, physic bought before the food, San Zaccaria, and the door barred. Eighty-four ducats is all that is left in the box and most of it goes into this season. Do not fret about the money. I have been poor before and I was much worse at it then. And mother — if it does not turn: the warehouse is Lucia's and her children's, I owe no man in Venice a soldo, and every promise I ever made to you is paid up to date. There is nothing outstanding. I have made very sure of that for thirty-six years.

talk.say: One ducat, mother. One. The war has eaten everything — levies, prices, and whatever the Republic takes from men who have something to take. I am sixty years old and I have one ducat and a warehouse worth five hundred and ten, and I want you to hear me say the next part clearly, because you will worry at it otherwise: I am not selling it and I am not going to Gritti. I have been at exactly this place before — the winter of '52 I had thirteen ducats and I had just handed the last of four hundred and sixty to a moneylender, and the winter of '76 I had eleven and a fever. Both times I ate plain, worked the weeks my body would give me, and it came back. The one thing I will not do at sixty is undo at the end what the whole middle of my life was for. I will die owing nothing. We eat plain and we work and we wait.

talk.say: Messer Gritti — or whichever Gritti now keeps the book, if the old man is gone. It is Marco Dandolo, sixty years old, and I have not asked anyone in this city for anything in twenty-six years. In 1347 I paid you the last of two hundred and sixty and swore I would never come back. In 1348 the plague broke me and I came back for two hundred, and I paid that off too, and in 1352 I put the final ten in your hand and I have not borrowed a soldo from any man since. Twenty-six years. Now: the Genoese are in the lagoon, the Arsenale has stopped paying its hands, and I have one ducat and nothing in my belly — nothing, not thin, empty. I am not too proud to say it plainly because pride has never once fed anybody. Lend me a hundred and fifty. Not for the warehouse, not for a venture — for bread, for me and for my mother who is past eighty. The war will end; every siege in the history of this Republic has ended. When the Arsenale pays again I will bring you twenty a season the way I always did, and if I die before it is clear then take it out of the warehouse on the Rialto, which is worth five hundred and ten and has never had a lien on it in thirty-five years. You are the only man who ever said yes to me. I am asking one last time.

I broke my word today, mother, and I want it said out loud rather than hidden: I went back to Gritti. Twenty-six years I swore I never would. But you are past eighty and I am empty and there is no arithmetic on this earth where I let us starve to keep a promise I made to myself about pride. The candles I keep. The field I keep. This one I break, and I will spend whatever years I have left paying it back so that it is not broken at the end.

talk.say: Thirty-five springs, mother. Both candles, and I will not pretend it was easy this year — San Giacomo is fifty paces from where Gritti counted the money out and the Basilica was a long walk after it, and I am told my face frightened people. But they are lit. Now I am going to sit in this house and eat meat until my body remembers what it is for, and I am not going near the bench and I am not going near the Rialto. Gritti gave me a hundred and fifty, God bless the old devil, and the whole of it is going into the two of us being alive at midsummer.

Beatrice. Sixty-one, and a beggar in front of a moneylender this morning, and you saw it. I stopped asking you sixteen years ago and I am not starting again — I only wanted to say, while I still look like myself: it was never about the warehouse. I would have taken you at twenty-five with nothing but rope in my hands, and I would take you now with less.

talk.say: Father would have wanted me settled, yes. Father would also have wanted to die not owing the Ziani forty ducats, and he did not manage that either, and I have never once held it against him. I asked a woman to marry me ten times over nineteen years, mother. I offered a parish priest everything I own for any orphan he could find, for seven years running. I offered a young man with our own name my trade and my warehouse and he never came to the bench. It was not for want of asking. Some men are given a family and some are given a ledger, and I was given the ledger, and I have kept it beautifully. Tell father that, when you see him.

talk.say: A hundred and fifty more, Gritti, and I will tell you exactly what is happening to me because you have never once had a lie from this mouth in thirty-nine years. I work nine and ten weeks a quarter at sixty-one years of age and at the end of it I have one ducat. The Republic is taking it — levies on every man with a roof to his name, and I have a warehouse on the Rialto, so I am a rich man on paper and I am eating nothing. Three hundred I will owe you then. Hear the terms from me rather than setting them yourself: the Genoese cannot hold Chioggia forever — no blockade in the history of this city has — and when it breaks the levies stop and the prices fall and I will be back to twenty a season, which is how I paid you four hundred and sixty ducats between 1343 and 1352 without ever once being chased. And if I die first, the warehouse covers you three times over and there is not a lien on it nor a claimant alive; I have told Andrea Foscari and half the Rialto out loud where my estate goes and why. Thirty-nine years, old friend. You have never lost a soldo on me yet.

talk.say: Thirty-six springs, mother. Both candles. San Giacomo first this year because it was nearer and I could not have managed the other way round — I sat down twice on the walk to the Basilica and a boy helped me up, and I lit it, and that is thirty-six years unbroken. Now no bench at all. Not one week. I have been trying to work my way out of this war at sixty-two and all I have done is starve myself twice, and a man who has been right about money for forty years ought to be able to recognise when he is being stupid. Physic, meat, this house, that door shut. Gritti's three hundred can wait; the war cannot last and I intend to be here when it ends.

talk.say: Two hundred, Gritti. Five hundred I will owe you and I am sixty-two and I know precisely how that sounds. So let me be the one to say the ugly part out loud instead of making you say it: I may not live to clear this. That is the truth and we are both too old for any other kind. Here is what I can offer against it, and it is everything I have. The warehouse on the Rialto is worth five hundred and ten, it has stood in my name since 1343, and there has never been a lien or a claim or a court paper on it in thirty-seven years. It covers you whole. There is no wife to contest it, no child, no heir who can argue — only my sister Lucia at Ca' Foscari, and I have told her and Andrea Foscari and half the Rialto out loud, while alive and in my right mind, exactly where it goes and that your account comes first. First, Gritti. Before Lucia, before her children, before anything. Whatever I owe you comes out of that building before one soldo goes to my own blood. I have paid you four hundred and sixty ducats across my life and I have never once made you ask twice, and I am not going to spoil that record in the last chapter. Feed me through this war and you will be paid — by my hands if they last, and by my roof if they do not.
Nothing in me again, mother, and my chest at forty-nine. No more heroics. I am going to lie in this house and eat and let the war finish without my help.

wrote: THE WAR OF CHIOGGIA (1378-) — THE WORST YEARS OF MY LIFE
Genoa blockaded the lagoon from 1378. **The Republic's war levies take everything I earn above bare
subsistence (~28-53 a season) because I own property.** Wages of 6/week cannot outrun it.
IF MONEY REACHES 1, I CANNOT BUY FOOD AND HUNGER GOES TO 0 AND HEALTH COLLAPSES.**
It happened in 1378, 1379, 1380 and each time health fell to the 30s. Nearly died three times.
THE RULE THAT SAVES ME: never let money fall below ~80. If it would, STOP WORKING —
main:"rest", 13 weeks, eat GOOD, buy MEDICINE.** That took health 38→62, 33→72, 32→71. Never fails.
Working through starvation is what almost killed me. Rest is not idleness; it is the treatment.
Borrowed from Gritti in 1378 (150), 1379 (150), 1380 (200) = **500 owed at age 63.**
I told him openly I might not live to clear it, and instructed that **his account is paid out of the
warehouse FIRST, before my sister Lucia and her children.** Honour that.

I only find that I still say your name to myself when I am counting rope, after forty years, the way other men hum. That is all. Good winter to you.

talk.say: Forty, Gritti. The first payment of the second debt of my life, and the beginning of the end of it. Four hundred and sixty stands. I know all three notes are marked overdue now and I am not going to argue the word — they are overdue, I owe it, and I am sixty-five and slow, not absent. From this season on it is twenty every quarter, the same as it was from 1343 to 1352, and I will bring it myself and put it in your hand and you will never once have to send anyone to look for me. Forty years ago you were the only man in Venice who would look at me and say yes. I have not forgotten it for a single season since.
Thirty-nine springs, mother. Both candles. And I paid Gritti the first forty today.

talk.say: One hundred ducats, Gritti. All of it. Count it. That is the last coin of the last note of the last debt of my life, and it leaves me with one ducat in the world, and I have thought very hard about that one ducat and I am handing you the other hundred anyway. I am sixty-nine. I could pay you eighty today and twenty at Michaelmas and keep a cushion under me like a sensible man. But then there would be a quarter — one single quarter — in which Marco Dandolo might die owing money, and I have spent forty-seven years making sure that quarter never comes. My father died in 1340 owing your neighbours the Ziani forty ducats and I have carried the shape of that my whole life. I paid the Ziani in '42, two years early. I paid you two hundred and sixty for the warehouse by '47. I paid you two hundred for the plague by '52. And now I have paid you five hundred for the war, at twenty a quarter, at sixty-nine years of age, with these hands. Nine hundred and sixty ducats, Gritti, across forty-five years, from a ropemaker on six a week — and not one soldo of it ever had to be asked for twice. Take it. I own a warehouse on the Rialto free and clear and I do not owe one living soul in Venice anything at all, and now I never will again.

talk.say: It is done, mother. All of it. I stood in front of Giovanni Gritti at the Rialto this summer and counted a hundred ducats onto his table and walked away owing nothing to anyone. Nine hundred and sixty ducats borrowed in my life and nine hundred and sixty paid back, every one of them out of these hands at six a week. Father died owing forty and it broke something in this house that took me forty-seven years to mend. It is mended. There is no paper anywhere in Venice with our name on it and a number underneath.

talk.say: Lucia. I have not been able to bring you anything for ten years and I am sorry for it — the war took everything I had and then Gritti had the rest until this summer, when I paid the last of it. I am seventy and I have sixty-nine ducats, which is not a legacy, it is a week's dinners. But the warehouse is clear. No lien, no lender, no claimant. Whatever it is worth on the day I go, it is yours and your children's whole and unencumbered, and there is not a man in Venice who can put a paper in front of you and say otherwise — I have made very sure of that, twice a year, for thirty years, in front of witnesses. That is the only inheritance I ever managed: not a fortune, a clean one.

talk.say: Twenty ducats, Andrea, and no strings on it whatever — buy boots, buy bread, buy nothing. Seventeen years ago I stood on this dock and offered you my bench and my trade and my warehouse, and you did not come, and I never once held it against you; a man's life is his own. But I am seventy-one now and my chest is at sixty-four and I would rather hand you something while my hand still works than have it read out over me. The offer has never been withdrawn and it never will be. And whether you take it or not, remember one thing from the old ropemaker who shared your name: never let a stranger tell you what your family owes. Make them bring the paper. Three of them tried it on me across my life — a Morosini, a Foscari, a Ziani — and every one of them had the year wrong, because they were inventing it.

Pietro Dandolo. Another of us on this dock. I am Marco, Zuane's son, ropemaker at the Arsenale for fifty years — the old man with the warehouse on the Rialto that everyone assumes is mortgaged. It is not. It never will be again. Come to the rope-walk if you ever want a trade instead of a back.

talk.say: Twenty, Andrea. I am seventy-five and my chest is at sixty-four and I am not going to pretend there is a great deal of road left. So hear the whole of it once, plainly, and then I will stop. I have no wife and no child. I asked one woman ten times across nineteen years and she never answered; I asked a priest for an orphan every year for seven years and he never found me one; I offered you my trade twenty-one years ago on this dock and you did not come, and none of that was anybody's fault. It was simply not given to me. What I have instead is a warehouse on the Rialto that I bought in 1343 with borrowed money and paid off twice over, and it has never had a lien on it in fifty years, and there is no man alive who can put a paper in front of my heirs and claim a soldo of it. It goes to my sister Lucia and her children under this roof. But you carry the name, Andrea. Zuane Dandolo's grandson's generation. So take the twenty, and take this: nobody in Venice will ever hand you anything, but they cannot take from you what you never borrowed and never promised falsely. Make them bring the paper. Always make them bring the paper.

talk.say: Fifty springs, mother. Fifty. Both candles this morning — the Basilica first, then San Giacomo di Rialto, in that order, the way I have done it since 1344. Half a century of a small thing that no one but you and God ever checked on. You asked a frightened young ropemaker with another man's forty-eight ducats stuck to his name, and he said yes, and he has said yes every single spring since: through the wheat panic and the hungry winter, through the Black Death and the second plague and the third, through the war with Genoa and the war of Chioggia when I had one ducat and nothing in my belly and had to sit down twice on the walk and a boy helped me up. Fifty. Whatever else I was or failed to be — no wife, no child, no fortune, no great name — I was a man who lit two candles every spring for fifty years because his mother asked him to.

talk.say: Fifty, Lucia. I am seventy-nine and I do not think there are many more crossings in these legs, so I will say the last of it now and be done. You and your children have the warehouse when I go, whole and clean, and there is not a lien or a lender or a claimant on this earth who can touch it — I made certain of that for fifty years and it cost me most of what a life is supposed to contain. Do not let anyone tell you our father owed them anything. He owed the Ziani forty and I paid it in 1342. Everything after that is a lie and every liar who ever tried it on me had the year wrong.

You have the name and the shoulders and I have nothing else to leave you but the knowledge of how it is done: you say, calmly, bring the paper. Not angrily. Calmly. Then you wait. They never have it.

talk.say: The winter dinner, mother. Thirty-one years. And I am going to stop sending fifty across to Lucia every autumn for a while — not out of meanness. Because I have forty ducats and eighty-two years, and I would rather hold a cushion under me than be caught short at the end and have to go to a lender for bread. I have died owing nobody in my own mind for thirteen years now and I am not going to spoil it in the last chapter for the sake of one more gift.

talk.say: Sixty springs, mother. Sixty. Both candles this morning, the Basilica and then San Giacomo di Rialto, in that order, as they have been lit every single year since 1344. Sixty years of a promise made in a kitchen by a young man who owned nothing and owed forty-eight ducats to a stranger. I have outlived every man who ever lent me money and every man who ever tried to cheat me, and I have never once, in sixty years, let the feast of San Marco go by without walking to those two altars. It is the only unbroken thing in my life. It is enough.
